The Atlantic chub mackerel Scomber colias attains a maximum recorded total length of 55 cm [Li = 55 cm], a size that places it among the smaller scombrid species within its genus. Field surveys conducted in the eastern Atlantic indicate that the length at which 50 percent of individuals have reached sexual maturity is 21.3 cm [Lp = 21.3 cm], a value derived from macroscopic gonad staging across multiple sampling seasons. The body mass corresponding to this pubertal length, calculated from the species-specific length-weight relationship (W = 0.00741 * L^3.03), is 78.5 grams [Wwp = 78.5 grams]. This relatively modest mass at maturity reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive investment over extended somatic growth, a pattern commonly observed in small pelagic fish subject to high natural mortality rates. Comparisons with other Scomber species, such as the chub mackerel's Atlantic congener Scomber scombrus, reveal that the pubertal length of 21.3 cm is slightly below the typical range for the genus, which tends toward later maturation in cooler waters.

Fertilised eggs of this species have a mean diameter of 1.05 mm, which yields an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.0006 grams [Wwb = 0.0006 grams] for the newly hatched prolarva. The onset of exogenous feeding in these yolk-sac larvae is critically dependent on water temperature, and under controlled rearing conditions at 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], hatching occurs within 2 days [ab = 2 days] of fertilisation. This rapid embryonic development of just two days is characteristic of warm-water scombrids and allows early transition to the planktonic larval phase. The hatchling mass of 0.0006 grams is among the lowest recorded for Atlantic scombrid species, reflecting the small egg size that in turn facilitates high fecundity at the population level. In contrast to many temperate-zone fish where embryonic development may extend for a week or more at lower temperatures, the brief incubation period of this mackerel facilitates multiple spawning events within a single breeding season.

At the other extreme of the life cycle, individuals can achieve a substantial adult body mass, with the theoretical maximum or ultimate wet weight calculated as 1390 grams [Wwi = 1390 grams] from the length-weight relationship. This corresponds to the asymptotic mass an individual would achieve after many years of growth, though in practice few individuals attain this size due to the high fishing mortality typical of exploited stocks. The oldest documented individuals in wild populations, based on otolith readings, have been recorded to reach a maximum lifespan of 18 years [am = 18 years] at a mean annual water temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C]. The considerable discrepancy between the rapid early growth to puberty and the prolonged later growth to asymptotic size underscores a growth trajectory that decelerates markedly after maturity. The ultimate wet weight of 1390 grams, when compared to the 78.5 gram mass at puberty, highlights that most of the species lifetime somatic investment occurs after the onset of reproductive capability.

Reproductive output in this species is remarkably high, reflecting its status as a batch-spawning small pelagic fish. Under the thermal conditions typical of optimal spawning (22.7 °C [T = 22.7 °C]), available data indicate that individual females produce approximately 1355 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 1355 eggs per day] during the peak spawning season. This represents the maximum daily reproduction rate observed, though total annual fecundity integrates spawning frequency and batch size across the extended breeding period. The high reproductive rate, which translates into a lifetime fecundity that can exceed half a million oocytes per female, is offset by extremely low egg and larval survival, a classic example of an r-selected life-history trade-off that maintains population stability under fluctuating environmental conditions typical of eastern Atlantic waters.

Temperature exerts a dominant influence on the early life history of this species. The incubation period from fertilisation to chorion rupture, as confirmed in laboratory studies, lasts 2 days [ab = 2 days] at 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], but extends considerably at cooler temperatures typical of the species' northern range. Similarly, the maximum lifespan estimated from growth models reaches 6570 days [am = 6570 days] when integrated over a lifetime mean temperature, with cooler conditions potentially slowing metabolic processes and extending longevity at a temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C]. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Scomber japonicus and Scomber scombrus confirm that Atlantic chub mackerel occupies an intermediate position in both growth rate and thermal tolerance, consistent with its distribution across temperate and subtropical waters of the Atlantic Ocean.
